verdict: Avoid new fertiliser exposure in Paradip until local demand and subsidy-cycle visibility improve; lend only to deregulated, non-subsidy product makers with tight structure.
title: Paradip Fertilisers: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A fertiliser unit here is a chemical converter: gas or imported ammonia, phosphoric acid and potash go in, urea, DAP and complex grades come out, and cash comes back through dealers and the subsidy chain.** Paradip's anchor is the IFFCO complex [2], with petrochemical feedstock and port linkages around it [1][3]. The money sits in two places: the subsidy receivable from the government, and dealer credit in the sowing season. **So when a proposal lands, check the split between subsidised and non-subsidised product; if subsidy receivable is more than a quarter of annual sales, ask for the claim-wise ageing and last three disbursement dates.**

## What has changed now
**The official data pack reads AVOID for this industry in this state, and the local signals are the reason.** Odisha GST collections grew +0.5% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D], and Odisha electricity demand grew +5.1% against India's +9.5% [D] — both point to slower local activity. Nationally, fertiliser output (NIC 20) fell -0.5% YoY and -1.2% Apr-to-date [D]. **So treat any Paradip proposal projecting volume growth above the state's own demand as unsupported; ask for the buyer list and the offtake contract behind the projection.**

## Where the growth is
**Peer results split cleanly: chemicals and deregulated products are earning, subsidised fertiliser is not.** Shree Pushkar's chemical segment revenue grew 38.1% YoY while its fertiliser segment fell 10.6% [4]; GSFC posted its highest-ever Q1 sales at Rs. 3,581 Cr with fertiliser sales up 82% [5]; Deepak's profit doubled on ammonia and industrial chemical realisations [6]. CRISIL expects complex fertiliser capacity to rise ~25% over ~16 MTPA in three fiscals [9]. **So pursue Paradip borrowers making customised, non-subsidised grades and industrial chemicals — the CARA note on Fertis India makes the point that less-regulated products sell across all four seasons, which smooths the working-capital cycle [8]. Avoid pure subsidy-dependent urea/DAP converters and traders with no captive conversion.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the receivable, not the inventory.** Keep tenor inside one subsidy cycle, take the subsidy claim and dealer receivables as primary security, and insist on a monthly stock-and-receivable statement plus monthly GST returns. **Take every month: subsidy claim status, dealer ageing, gas/ammonia input price, and capacity utilisation.** Where the borrower sells deregulated products, a quarterly segment margin is enough; where subsidy dominates, monthly. **If the borrower cannot show claim disbursement within the cycle, decline rather than extend.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the local demand pulse first.** A second consecutive month of Odisha GST growth below India's [D] means stop new sanctions in the cluster. **Watch the subsidy receivable ageing — past two cycles unpaid means restructure or exit.** Watch dealer credit stretching beyond the season, and any shift of sales to related parties. Peer commentary flags volatile global input and pricing [5][6]; a sharp input price move with fixed selling price is a margin call, so ask for the pass-through clause before disbursal.

## Local evidence is thin
**The local sources are topic pages, not deal-level reporting [1][2][3]; the rating reports carry no date [8][10][11], so treat them as background only.** Lean on first principles and the peer set above.

## The call
**Avoid new fertiliser exposure in Paradip now; the data pack scores it AVOID and the Odisha demand signals are weaker than India's [D].** Lend only to deregulated-product converters with monthly receivable discipline.
